pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–7 years

- **Topic:** What Is a Volcano

- **Standards — UK (DfE, England):** England places volcanoes in the **KS2 Geography** programme of study (ages 7–11: 'describe and understand key aspects of physical geography, including … volcanoes and earthquakes'), NOT in KS1 science; at this 5–7 band there is no statutory volcano content. Teach as early Earth-science enrichment supported by KS1 science 'Working scientifically' (observing closely, asking simple questions, using simple information sources).

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No K–2 performance expectation names volcanoes directly; the nearest anchor is **2-ESS1-1** ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS1-1]'), whose clarification names 'volcanic explosions … which happen quickly' — so a volcano is the canonical example of a fast Earth event. Foreshadows grade-4 ESS2 (Earth's surface processes/geosphere).

- **Operational details:** At 5–7 the goal is a clear mental picture, not mechanism: a volcano is an opening in the ground where very hot, melted rock comes out. The single most important idea to establish is that **lava is rock so hot it has melted** — not fire, not a special liquid. Build from vivid real photos/footage (a red-glowing lava flow, an ash cloud) and a simple labelled cross-section: the mountain, the opening at the top, the lava coming out. Use the everyday-material bridge from Y1 ('rock is a material') so 'melted rock' is graspable. Keep magma-vs-lava, chambers and vents for the 7–9 'Inside a Volcano' topic; here, name what a child can point to and see. Give the child language to narrate a picture ('the hot melted rock — lava — is coming out of the opening').

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, ≈5–7, KS1). Children can recognise and name a volcano and say hot melted rock comes out; they should NOT yet be expected to explain WHY (plate boundaries, magma chambers) — that is later. Watch the dominant young misconception that the glowing lava is 'fire': explicitly say it is melted rock that glows because it is so hot.
bestPractices: Anchor on vivid real imagery/footage first (a glowing lava flow, an ash plume) so the concept is concrete before any diagram
Lead with the core correction 'lava is melted ROCK, not fire' — say it, show glowing lava cooling into solid black rock
Use a simple labelled cross-section with only three parts a child can point to: mountain, opening (top), lava coming out
Bridge from Y1 everyday materials ('rock is a material') so 'melted rock' is believable rather than magical
Give sentence frames to narrate a picture ('hot melted rock — lava — is coming out of the opening') to meet the 'point and describe' evidence
Defer magma/chamber/vent vocabulary and eruption mechanism to the 7–9 topics; keep this purely definitional
keyRepresentations: Labelled volcano cross-section (mountain, opening/vent, lava flow, ash cloud)
Before-and-cooled pair: glowing orange lava → solid black rock (lava is rock)
Real photographs/footage of an erupting volcano
A simple 'opening in the ground' schematic that de-emphasises the mountain (not all volcanoes are tall cones)
commonMisconceptions: 'The glowing lava is fire' — it is rock so hot it has melted and glows; there is no burning flame in the flow
'A volcano is a mountain that breathes fire / a fire-breathing monster' — it is an opening in Earth's surface where melted rock comes out
'All volcanoes are tall pointed mountains' — the defining feature is the opening, not the cone shape
'Lava comes straight from the centre of the Earth' — at this age keep it to 'from hot melted rock underground'; deep structure comes later
'Volcanoes only existed long ago / are not real now' — many volcanoes are active today

learn.summary: For 5–7 year-olds, establish a clear mental picture of a volcano: an opening in Earth's surface where hot melted rock (lava) comes out. The single most important idea is that lava is ROCK so hot it has melted and glows because of its heat — not fire, not a burning flame, and not some separate special liquid different from rock. Keep the work definitional (recognise, name, describe); defer magma chambers, vents, plate boundaries and eruption mechanism to later (7–9) topics. Build from vivid real imagery and a simple three-part labelled cross-section, and give children sentence frames to narrate what they see.

activities.title: Tap-and-name the volcano picture
feedback: If the child calls the lava 'fire', point to the zoom-in: lava glows because it is very hot, not because it is burning; watch the same lava cool into hard black rock.
If the child names only the mountain, note that the defining feature is the opening where lava comes out — not every volcano is a tall pointed cone.
Praise a full narration that names lava as 'melted rock' and points to the opening it comes from.
activities.rationale: The learning target is recognition and vocabulary ('point to a volcano and describe what is happening'), so a labelled illustration with tap-to-reveal parts supplies the naming and the key correction. The lift-the-flap and cooling zoom-in make the 'melted rock, not fire' idea concrete and seed the later idea that cooled lava becomes solid rock. The specific interactions (tap-to-name, lift-the-flap, drill-down zoom) are illustrative proposals, not mandatory or independently validated.
sourceClaims: Lava is molten rock that reaches the surface (magma once erupted); it glows because it is extremely hot, not because it is on fire
learnerActions: Look at a large, friendly cross-section of an erupting volcano (mountain, opening at the top, lava flowing down, ash cloud).
Tap each part to hear/read a short naming phrase: 'the mountain', 'the opening at the top', 'the lava coming out', 'the ash cloud (tiny bits of rock, not ash from burning)'.
Open a lift-the-flap sitting on the lava: front asks 'What is lava?', the flap reveals 'Rock so hot it has MELTED — it glows because it is hot, it is not fire.'
Zoom in on a close-up where a blob of glowing orange lava cools and hardens into solid black rock.
Narrate the whole picture aloud using a sentence frame: 'The hot melted rock — lava — is coming out of the opening.'
activities.intendedInsight: A volcano is an opening where hot melted rock comes out; lava is rock that has melted and glows because it is so hot, and it cools back into solid rock.

activities.title: Press to erupt
feedback: If the child says fire is coming out, replay and point to the cooled black rock at the edges: lava is rock that cools and hardens, which fire does not do.
Keep attention on the one action (lava coming out and cooling); avoid pulling in eruption causes, which come later.
activities.rationale: An eruption animation can make 'hot melted rock comes out' felt through action and is motivating at this age. It is offered as an alternative to the static picture with a different purpose: it dramatises the 'comes out' idea, while the labelled image more directly secures naming/vocabulary. Limit it to a single action so it stays definitional and does not drift into eruption-mechanism territory (a 7–9 topic). Live recolouring from orange to black is an illustrative way to show cooling, not a required feature.
sourceClaims: Lava is molten rock that reaches the surface (magma once erupted); it glows because it is extremely hot, not because it is on fire
learnerActions: Tap the volcano to make it erupt: watch lava well up at the opening and flow down the sides.
Watch the lava cool from bright orange at the top to solid black rock at the cooled edges.
Read the caption that names the flowing stuff 'lava'.
Say in your own words where the lava is coming out and what happens as it cools.
activities.intendedInsight: Hot melted rock comes OUT of the opening of a volcano, and as it flows away and cools it hardens into solid rock.

activities.title: Melt-and-cool prediction (hands-on check)
feedback: If the child predicts the wax 'burns up' or 'turns into fire', that signals the 'hot and glowing = burning' idea; the melt-and-cool demonstration shows it softens and then hardens back into a solid.
Treat the reason given BEFORE melting as the diagnostic part — it reveals whether the child thinks 'hot = burning' or 'hot = a melted solid'.
Affirm the correct idea: it melts to a soft/runny state and then hardens back into a solid. Note that, unlike lava, the wax or chocolate is not hot enough to glow.
activities.rationale: A predict–observe–explain task with a familiar meltable solid targets the dominant misconception that lava is fire. The pre-melting reason surfaces the child's model; the observed cooling-and-hardening provides counter-evidence. Wax and chocolate are everyday approximations, not rock, and are not hot enough to glow; name them as stand-ins for how a hot solid melts and re-solidifies. This is a proposed task, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Lava is molten rock that reaches the surface (magma once erupted); it glows because it is extremely hot, not because it is on fire
learnerActions: Look at a solid piece of wax or chocolate.

Before anything happens, PREDICT: if we heat it until it flows like lava and then let it cool, will it (a) burn up into ash, (b) turn into fire, or (c) become solid again — and say WHY. (Then we test it to see what really happens.)
An adult gently warms it (for example in a bowl over warm water, away from any flame) until it flows, then let it cool, and check what actually happens.

Connect it back: like lava, a hot melted solid can flow while it is hot and then harden back into a solid when it cools. Lava is far hotter, so lava also glows; the wax or chocolate is not hot enough to glow.

Answer the probes: 'If the glowing lava cools right down, what does it turn into?', 'Where does the melted rock come from — the top of the mountain, or from hot melted rock underground?', and 'Is the volcano hot because something is burning, or for a different reason?'
activities.intendedInsight: Glowing and hot does not mean burning: a melted solid flows while hot and hardens again when cooled, just as lava (melted rock) cools into solid rock. The wax/chocolate shows melting and re-solidifying; the glow is a feature of lava's extreme heat, not of the stand-in.

activities.title: Quick recognition check
feedback: The 'fire' option is the teachable distractor: if chosen, revisit the melt-and-cool evidence that lava is rock that cools and hardens.

Because 'it's fire' and 'it's melted rock' both seem to explain the orange glow, follow up by asking what the orange stuff IS and where it comes from — a child holding the fire idea talks about burning and flames instead of 'melted rock from underground'.
activities.rationale: A short selected-response check can confirm recognition and key vocabulary, with the 'fire' distractor exposing the target misconception. Recognition-only responses confirm the child can pick and name but do not by themselves build the picture or elicit the child's own narration, so use this after teaching rather than as a first encounter.
learnerActions: Choose from pictures: 'Which picture shows a volcano?'
Answer 'What is lava?' choosing from melted rock / fire / water (melted rock is correct).
Respond to a friend who says 'That's fire coming out of the mountain' — agree or disagree, and say what the orange stuff really is and where it comes from.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirm the child can recognise a volcano and state that lava is melted rock, not fire or water.

constraints: Keep the topic purely definitional at 5–7: name what a child can point to and see. Defer magma-vs-lava, chambers, vents, plate boundaries and eruption causes to the 7–9 'Inside a Volcano' topics.
Children at this band should recognise and name a volcano and say hot melted rock comes out; they are NOT yet expected to explain WHY eruptions happen.
Explicitly address the dominant misconception that glowing lava is 'fire': say it is melted rock that glows because it is so hot, and show lava cooling into solid black rock.

Also watch for 'a volcano is a fire-breathing mountain/monster', 'all volcanoes are tall pointed cones', 'lava comes straight from the centre of the Earth' (keep to 'from hot melted rock underground'), and 'volcanoes only existed long ago' (many are active today).
The recognition check confirms naming but does not elicit the child's own narration or build the initial picture; use it after the picture/eruption/hands-on work.

Wax and chocolate are everyday stand-ins for a meltable solid, not actual rock; they model melting and re-solidifying only and are NOT hot enough to glow — the glow is a feature of lava's extreme temperature, so do not describe the wax/chocolate as glowing.
Bridge from the Year 1 idea that 'rock is a material' so 'melted rock' is believable rather than magical.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source marks the NGSS 2-ESS1-1 claim as verified:true and the DfE curriculum and USGS lava-basics claims as verified:false; confidence was logged as 'high'. Treat the unverified claims accordingly; no fresh verification has been performed.

The original row's assessment described the melted wax/chocolate as a 'glowing-soft liquid'; this is inaccurate for these low-temperature materials and has been corrected so the stand-in models melting/solidifying only, with glowing reserved for lava.

Source artefact ratings asserted that '3D adds nothing' and that conversation/dialogue is unsuitable here. These are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical facts, and are not reproduced as universal claims. A spoken discussion or model can still support teaching; the point retained is only that a labelled picture reliably secures naming at this age.

The legacy row called the labelled-image approach the single reliable way to secure the vocabulary; this rewrite keeps the eruption animation and hands-on predict-observe-explain as alternatives with distinct purposes rather than treating any one medium as necessary.

assess.poeTask: Show the child a solid piece of wax or chocolate. Before doing anything, ask them to PREDICT: if we heat it until it flows like lava and then let it cool, will it (a) burn up into ash, (b) turn into fire, or (c) become solid again — and WHY? A child who thinks lava is fire predicts it burns away or flames; the correct prediction is that it melts to a glowing-soft liquid and then hardens back into a solid. Melt and cool it to check. The reason given before melting is the diagnostic part — it reveals whether they think 'hot and glowing = burning' or 'hot = a melted solid'.
probeDeeper: If we let the glowing orange lava cool right down, what would it turn into?
Where does the melted rock come from — the top of the mountain, or deep down inside the Earth?
Is the volcano hot because something is burning, or for a different reason?
Point to the volcano in this picture and tell me what is happening.
assess.correctAnswer: The friend is wrong — it isn't fire. It's lava: rock from deep inside the Earth that got so hot it melted into a runny, glowing liquid. A volcano is an opening where this hot melted rock comes out, and when lava cools it turns back into hard rock.

errorPatterns.pattern: The orange stuff is fire — the volcano is burning ('the mountain's on fire')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront it — melt then cool a solid (wax/chocolate): glowing means hot, not burning, and lava cools into hard rock.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's fire coming out of the mountain.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the lava fire or flames and talks about burning.

errorPatterns.pattern: Lava is a special hot liquid, not rock — and stays liquid forever
errorPatterns.nextMove: It's the SAME rock, just melted; when it cools it becomes hard rock again — show a lava-rock sample.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's a special hot liquid, not rock.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies lava is rock, or thinks it never turns solid.

errorPatterns.pattern: The volcano 'breathes' or makes fire like a dragon
errorPatterns.nextMove: A volcano is an opening in the ground, not a creature; the heat comes from melted rock deep down.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the volcano as alive, breathing or blowing fire.

responseLevels.gap: Calls it fire or says the mountain is burning; can't say what lava is.
responseLevels.full: Identifies it as lava — melted rock from inside the Earth that glows because it's hot, not fire — knows it cools into solid rock, and points to the volcano as the opening it comes from.
responseLevels.partial: Says 'lava' and knows it's hot, but still thinks it's fire or isn't sure it's melted rock.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: This picture shows a volcano with glowing orange stuff pouring down it. A friend says, 'That's fire coming out of the mountain.' Do you agree? What is the orange stuff really, and where does it come from?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 'It's fire' and 'it's melted rock' both seem to explain the orange glow, so the first-tier answer alone doesn't separate them. Asking what the orange stuff IS and where it comes from forces 'melted rock from inside the Earth' — a child holding the fire idea talks about burning and flames instead.
